title: Peter's three denials (Luke 22:54–62)
hookLine: a servant girl asks, a cock crows, and the Lord turns and looks at Peter

cards: It's the middle of the night. Jesus has been arrested and taken into the high priest's house. Peter, the one who said he'd go to prison and to death with him, has followed at a distance, all the way into the courtyard.
Somebody has lit a fire. It's cold. Peter sits down with the others around it, trying to look like everyone else.
A servant girl looks at him in the firelight. Looks again. And says, to the whole circle, this man was with him too.
Peter answers before he thinks. In the Douay-Rheims: "Woman, I know him not." That's the first one.

teach.b: Luke tells it in three quick blows. The girl. A little later, another person: you're one of them.
Peter: I am not. About an hour on, a third insists: this man was with him, for he's a Galilean too. And Peter says he doesn't even know what the man is talking about.
While he's still speaking, a rooster crows.

teach.h: THE LORD TURNING LOOKED ON PETER.
teach.b: Then the verse only Luke has: "And the Lord turning looked on Peter." Jesus is somewhere in that courtyard, under guard, close enough to turn.
Peter remembers what Jesus told him at supper: before the cock crowed, he would deny him three times. "And Peter going out, wept bitterly."

teach.h: THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY WHAT THE LOOK WAS.
teach.b: Here's the honest part: Luke never tells us what that look was like. Christians have read it for centuries as mercy, not anger, because of what comes after. Peter isn't written off.
On Easter morning, Luke says, he's the one who runs to the tomb.
And this is the same Peter Jesus called the rock.

teach.h: AND PETER GOING OUT, WEPT BITTERLY.
teach.b: The first pope, in Catholic teaching, is a man who failed his friend three times in one night and was not given up on. The Church was built on someone who knew exactly how much he needed mercy.
That's why Catholics say a failure is never the last word, and why they say confession exists: you go out, you weep, and you come back.

how: Catholics hear the story of Peter's denial in the Passion read on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, and many bring their own failures to God in the sacrament of confession.

games.q: you're Peter. the rooster has just crowed and he has turned and looked at you. what do you do?
games.why: "and Peter going out, wept bitterly." he weeps, and on Easter morning he runs to the tomb. Catholics call him the first pope.

practice: Let one real moment come back when you let a friend down, not the worst one: a time you went quiet when you should have spoken, or said you didn't know someone you did.
Don't argue with it; let it be true, then picture a look coming toward you across the courtyard, not anger, something that knows and stays. If you pray, you can ask for mercy in your own plain words.

wordCard.voice: rooster. Its crow caught Peter mid-denial, and then the Lord turned and looked at him across the courtyard.

orig.note: Greek: to deny, to say no, to disown. the verb used for Peter's three denials.
